#5684. These Are The Cars You Want Robert Pattinson's James Bond To Drive

Robert Pattinson is James Bond. It's an unexpected casting, but likely a good one — Pattinson loves to get weird with a role, and that's exactly what Bond needs after the gritty Craig movies. Every Bond movie needs a Bond car, though, and we haven't yet seen what Pattinson will drive in his first outing in the role. That's why, earlier this week, I asked you all what car Robert Pattinson should drive as Bond. Today, we're looking through your answers.

Some of you picked genuinely good spy cars, like a beat-up Nissan Altima. Others went for more of the Mr. Bean approach with an Aston Martin Cygnet. Still some of you appear to have just stepped out of a 20-year coma, and only know Pattinson from "Twilight" rather than "Primetime," "The Odyssey," "Mickey 17," "The Batman," "Tenet," "The Lighthouse," "Good Time," or any other movie he's been fantastic in since his last appearance as Edward Cullen 14 years ago. Let it rest, y'all.

Should be a Volvo C30, because it would be a full circle from the first Twilight movie and that would amuse me.

We can incorporate driving a classic car into the plot. First he drives that new electric Jag with all the spy features, lasers, mines, machine guns etc. Then it gets hacked and driven off a bridge and Bond almost dies. After recovering, he drives a DB5 that can't be hacked.

Has to be an Aston Martin. Needs to be unique and stylish, but also manage to blend in when needed.

2014 Altima complete with damaged left quarter panel and duck taped rear bumper. No one will ever know he's a spy.

In this day and age? An Uber. Don't want to attract attention by driving the same car past Flock cameras all the time.

James Bond is usually reflective of his era. Sean Connery was peak cold war and peak Mad Men era. Pierce Brosnan was lighter, post cold war who looked and acted like a 90s banker investing in pre-tech crash stocks. Daniel Craig was the Global War on Terror Bond, a bruiser who could have back back from two tours in Afghanistan.

Robert Pattinson is the post GWOT Bond. From looking up pictures of him (I had no idea who he was until they announced it) he's less built up and less brooding than Daniel Craig, probably closer to a Pierce Brosnan Bond. I'd expect more sophistication (a British prep school backstory, not an orphan with a murky past), less hand to hand combat, probably more tech forward than Daniel Craig's Bond.

Bad guys will either be AI, Russia (a Putin analogue) or a combination of the two. It won't be China because Amazon will want to sell tickets in China/stream in China so it'll have to get past Chinese censors.

So expect the new Bond's ride to be something British, sleep, and sophisticated that wouldn't look out of place in a country club parking lot. Not one of Aston Martin's more hard-core variants but a gentleman's express with four seats, an opponent interior, and a plush ride. Probably Aston, maybe Range Rover, possible Rolls Royce.

Bond should drive a 5th gen Civic Type R. It was built in Britain, so it's got that covered.

However, he's a spy. He needs to maintain a low profile. Hence, Civic.

It's got to be an Aston Martin. It can't be the Valkyrie or the Valhalla. Those are too hard for the "Bond girl" to get in and out of in a dress. The Valen and the Valiant are both limited editions and would make good movie cars, but they're both a little too boy-racer for Bond. At the end of the day, a DB12 is the Bond car. It's long and lean, it has lots of room for gadgets, it's got class for days, and it's got a screaming V12 for when things get spirited. You can fight bad guys in it, then roll up to the opera.

Depends on the tone of the movie. If he's looking to drive something outrageous and have a 200mph chase, he'll drive a new Aston Martin Valhalla.

Something sophisticated to take to somewhere in a European city where you can only enter by birthright due to your great-great-great-grandfather saving someone in a war, the Aston Martin Valen.

— Paul Offit and Noel Brewer discuss the measles resurgence and what it will take to reverse course

What does it mean for the U.S. to lose its measles elimination status after more than 25 years -- and what will it take to regain it?

In this 45-minute webinar, MedPage Today Editor-in-Chief Jeremy Faust, MD, speaks with pediatric infectious disease expert Paul Offit, MD, of Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, and public health researcher Noel Brewer, PhD, of the University of North Carolina in Chapel Hill, about the nation's loss of measles elimination status. #5682. MG U9 EV Ute — It’s A Monster Truck

We visit the MG dealership and get to know the MG U9 EV ute up close and personal.

As I have said many times to CleanTechnica readers, Australia needs more BEV utes. The PHEV utes are taking a bite out of diesel sales, but we need some monster truck battery electrics to push electrification deep into the heart of the bush-bashing Aussie tradie. I think that MG may have achieved that with the launch of the MG U9 EV. Yesterday, Majella and I went to have a look. Even Russell Coight would be impressed and the Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV should be feeling threatened. Take a break and watch the funny video. I doubt it will affect the sales of the Shark though.

So, yesterday, Majella I set out to have an adventure visiting the various car yards near our home. We were actually planning to look at some new electric vans, but ended up in the MG showroom with a very knowledgeable sales rep exploring the MG U9 EV. What a surprise! An early morning google search assured me that there were none in Brisbane available to view. This dealership not only brought one out from the pre-delivery area for us to check out, but also told us they had already sold and delivered their first one and had six more on order.

The MG U9 EV (it also comes in diesel) is joining the thin ranks of BEV utes already available in Australia — the KGM Musso and the Toyota Hilux BEV. So far this year, 269 KGM Mussos have sold in Australia. 174 MG U9 EVs are listed as delivered, possibly mainly to dealers. The cost of the MG U9 EV is approximately AU$80,000, just a few thousand more than the Toyota Hilux BEV. The diesel version of the MG sells for around AU$50,000.

The sales rep told me about his first customer for the MG ute: “He was keen. He already had home solar and a battery and was producing far more electricity than he could use. His solution: trade in the old diesel ute on a U9 EV ‘rolling battery.’ It will complement his Kia EV6. With the 6.6 kWh of the U9 vehicle-to-load [capability], he plans to power his house.” The ecosystem expands. For those with a query, it is not worth selling power back to the grid.

The MG U9 has a 102.2 kWh LFP battery, big enough to give a range of up to 430 km and send this behemoth hurtling down the road — accelerating to 100 km an hour from zero in 5.8 seconds. That’s as fast as my new Tesla! And an advertised top speed of 190 km/hour. Just as well it has disc brakes all round — with the front ones ventilated. And to recharge — 42 minutes from 20–80%.

Tare weight comes in at 2815 kg, towing capacity is 3500 kg, and it has the capacity to carry 685 kg in the tray. Unladen ground clearance is listed as 230 mm, and it has a wading depth of 550 mm. Length is 5500 mm; width 2265 mm; height 1874 mm. Very similar dimensions to the GMC Hummer with half the battery capacity. Hummer: L 5507 mm; W 2201 mm; H 2055 mm.

The MG U9 BEV includes a fold-down rear bulkhead to extend cargo-bed length inside the cabin, plus a 1,200 L tub capacity and a 236 L front trunk (frunk).

Google tells me: “The MG U9 EV Dual-Cab Ute comes equipped from the factory with a four-wheel electronic air suspension system offering over 100 mm of vertical height adjustment (including an Off-Road Lift mode, and automatic lowering by -20 mm at 80 km/h and -40 mm at 120 km/h.”

Of course there is a lot more to know, especially about tech and safety features. I am just whetting your appetite. You can find out more here. Or watch a video review on YouTube here.

At the moment, the dealership is fielding 8 enquiries a week online, but it is expecting some headwinds in mid 2027 when the Australian federal government is planning to review Fringe Benefit Tax benefits for electric vehicles. My comment was that somehow car manufacturers seem to find ways of reducing costs when government support is modified.

While I peppered the sales rep with questions, Majella did her usual photographic exploration and analysis.

She was impressed by the massive frunk, as was I — you could fit a whole body in there! The frunk can be opened from the outside by a physical button.

… and it has a power point for your fridge or coffeemaker!

The ute features doors with physical buttons and handles for ease of access.

The gear lever reminded Majella of the ones we see in the cockpit of a plane.

A variety of charging options for your tech are provided: cigarette lighter, USB charger, and more.

Perhaps MG went overboard with buttons — lots of physical buttons on the dash and on the steering wheel, plus the screen. Majella thought that this was a comfortable wheel size and shape for a long drive.

Behind the back seats in a cubby hole we have the charge cords: a trickle charger and type 2 to type 2.

The back tailgate has a discreet button to push to fold it down so you can load the tray.

An emergency glass breaker and a seat belt cutter is provided.

Although MG appears to have thought of everything, Majella commented that the only thing they don’t supply is a first aid kit.

The air suspension is easily adjusted air suspension from the centre screen. The sales rep confided that the staff were playing with it the day before.

The 360 degree camera extends to the trailer, with an aerial view for easily reversing.

Those looking for a truck to haul stuff, power their tools, and store excess energy would do well to consider the MG U9 EV. It may not be a Hummer, but it’s close. For tradies and bush bashers, the future can now be bright and electric.

David Waterworth is a retired teacher who divides his time between looking after his grandchildren and trying to make sure they have a planet to live on. He is long on Tesla [NASDAQ:TSLA].

#5681. 2027 Genesis G80 And GV80 Hybrids Launch In The U.S. With 347 HP And Much Better Fuel Economy

We have been eagerly awaiting the arrival of Genesis' first full-on hybrid option for a while, as it's been one of the only luxury brands not to launch such a powertrain. The GV80 Hybrid was finally shown off in Korea in August, and now on Thursday at the Los Angeles Auto Show, Genesis has revealed that midsize crossover in U.S.-spec form and held the world premiere of the the even cooler G80 Hybrid sedan, too.

The GV80 and G80 Hybrids will share the same powertrain, which pairs a turbocharged 2.5-liter inline-4 gasoline engine with a 7-speed automatic transmission, a single electric motor and a battery pack of unknown size. It's Hyundai Motor Group's first hybrid system with a liquid-cooled battery, and the system produces a combined 347 horsepower while returning Genesis-claimed efficiency gains of 24% in the GV80 and 30% in the G80, compared to the regulas gas-only models. Official fuel economy estimates for these two hybrids are not available just yet, but Genesis says both the GV80 SUV and G80 sedan should return a maximum driving range of over 500 miles on a tank of gas.

Genesis says its turbo hybrid system was "engineered specifically to highlight the brand's longitudinal, rear-wheel-drive-based architecture," and the liquid-cooled battery allows for a higher maximum discharge output when compared to air-cooled batteries. We've already sampled a version of Hyundai Motor Group's turbo-hybrid powertrain in the segment-topping Hyundai Palisade Hybrid. Jalopnik's own Andy Kalmowitz praised that version of the powertrain for its seamless transitions between electric and hybrid operation, which bodes well for the Genesis system and its upgrades.

In Genesis form, this hybrid setup produces 347 horsepower and 391 pound-feet of torque, which is 18 more horses and 52 more lb-ft of torque than the Palisade's Hybrid system. It's also 47 horsepower more than the G80 and GV80's base turbocharged 2.5-liter four-cylinder powertrain, and it matches the torque output of the top twin-turbo 3.5-liter V6, which Genesis says helps give it "responsive acceleration from a stop."

Both the GV80 and G80 Hybrids will offer buyers adjustable regenerative braking settings, a nice features that is not always found on traditional hybrids, and it has a Smart function that automatically adjusts regenerative braking based on driving conditions. They also have a Stay mode that allows some auxiliary functions like the climate control and multimedia functions to operate without starting the gas engine.

Both the GV80 Hybrid and G80 Hybrid sedan get a redesigned front grille with a new 3D look, new wheel designs, and new exterior colors. The GV80 has new 19-, 20-, and 22-inch wheel designs developed specifically for the Hybrid, and three new exterior colors: Seychelles Beige, Cardiff Green, and Brunswick Green Matte. It also will come with four new two-tone interior color combinations, real wood trim options, and upholstery quilting patterns.

The G80 Hybrid reflects a bigger change when compared to its gasser siblings: it's actually 5.1 inches longer overall than other G80s. Though Genesis doesn't explicitly say where the G80 Hybrid's extra 5.1 inches goes, it's almost certainly a 5.1-inch wheelbase stretch, since that's the same change that was made to the 2027 Genesis G80 Electrified in other markets. (That car was quietly canceled in the U.S. last year due to slow sales, if you'll remember, so we haven't gotten the LWB G80 until now.) That means it will have a limo-like wheelbase of 123.6 inches, or just 1.6 inches shorter than the flagship Genesis G90 sedan. The G80 Hybrid also gets new 18- and 20-inch wheel designs, and new exterior paint options that are inspired by locations and natural elements from around the world like Wadden Gray, Milos Blue, and Barolo Red.

These new hybrids will provide Genesis buyers with a third powertrain option on both cars, and they'll each be sold in the usual array of trim levels. Standard features include a 27-inch OLED gauge cluster and infotainment screen, and an array of standard active safety features. Genesis hasn't released official North American pricing or availability for either hybrid yet, but we expect pricing to fall between their base turbocharged four-cylinder powertrains and the more expensive twin-turbocharged V6, so somewhere around $70,000 for both models.

#5680. Novel ADC Could Expand Treatment Options in Ovarian Cancer

— Torvutatug samrotecan may benefit patients across folate receptor alpha expression levels

Updated results from the FONTANA trial presented at the annual European Society for Medical Oncology congress showed promising activity with the investigational antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) torvutatug samrotecan (torvu-sam) in patients with previously treated ovarian cancer, including those with low or absent folate receptor alpha expression.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, Funda Meric-Bernstam, MD, of the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, discusses the findings and how torvu-sam could expand treatment options for a broader patient population, including its potential role alongside existing therapies and in future treatment settings.

Following is a transcript of her remarks:

FONTANA is looking at torvu-sam, which is a folate receptor antibody-drug conjugate. This is an antibody-drug conjugate that targets folate receptor and has a topoisomerase payload. This trial had presented at ESMO 2025 where the dose escalation had been shared, and this was updated data in that we had further follow-up on our dose optimization, and we'd also included a cohort of patients that had ultra-low or null expression of folate receptor. So these were results from 156 patients that had been previously treated and now getting this antibody-drug conjugate.

The class of topoisomerase ADCs I think are really emerging as an exciting therapeutic opportunity. And we were pleased to see the activity in the folate receptor expression-high cohort where the objective response rate was 61.7%. But also we enrolled patients that had folate receptor expression low, and in that patient population, the response rate was 57%. We also enrolled a group of patients that had shorter follow-up, but the objective response rate in the folate receptor expression ultra-low or null was 48%.

So overall, this was also notable that these responses were quite durable. And we reported in the folate receptor-high group, their durability was 10.2 months, with the folate receptor-low group being 8.3 months. So overall the PFS [progression-free survival] in the high group was 9.7 months and the low was 7.6 months. Taken together to suggest that really this is an active agent that has no new safety signals, adverse events consistent with the topoisomerase ADC mechanism of action.

These are different-mechanism-of-action ADCs. Mirvetuximab [soravtansine (Elahere)], of course, has a different safety profile as well, but notably patients need to have folate receptor expression tested and they need to have 75% tumor cell positivity for that monotherapy activity. So here, the fact that we saw activity in the low cohort, which had 25% of the tumor cells positive, as well as the ultra-low/null cohort, that really makes it a lot more promising because feasibly we could offer this therapy even without testing and a lot larger patient population will be able to benefit from this agent.

Currently, ongoing clinical trials are looking at torvu-sam in comparison with mirvetuximab in patients that are fully receptor-high, also comparing torvu-sam in patients... in fully super-low with standard chemotherapy, as well as looking at torvu-sam in the maintenance setting.

This is a really exciting time. We're learning more about how we can better target cell surface antigens, and I think topoisomerase inhibitors really have a great opportunity to be impactful in a much larger patient population.

#5679. 2027 Hyundai Elantra Feels Too Nice To Be Treated Like An Economy Car

For the most part, economy cars are treated as fairly disposable pieces of equipment meant mostly for getting folks from Point A to Point B. They're not exactly treated with much care during their lives, and when they're used up, they're scuttled off to the nearest junkyard. More likely than not, that same fate will befall the 2027 Hyundai Elantra and 2028 Elantra Hybrid, and I don't think that's fair. Top to bottom and front to back, this little sedan is just far too nice to deserve a fate like that.

As with the redesigned Tucson, Hyundai put its entire back into its eighth-generation compact sedan, giving it a distinct and decidedly upmarket look, a premium-feeling interior, a cutting-edge brain with stellar interior tech, and a hybrid powertrain that'll get over 50 mpg, all while maintaining the idea that "affordability is standard," according to Olabisi Boyle, Hyundai's Senior VP of product planning and mobility strategy. While I haven't driven it yet, the slightly larger new Elantra seems mighty impressive when it comes to the design, feel and specs.

Full Disclosure: Hyundai paid for my food and transportation so I could check out the new Elantra and Tucson at a warehouse in Jersey City, New Jersey.

The first thing about the new Elantra that will jump out at you about is undoubtedly how it looks. It's the latest example of Hyundai's "Art of Steel" design language that we've previously seen on the China-only Ioniq V, Boulder concept and recently revealed Tucson. Hyundai also told me that the Elantra's design pulls from the N Vision 74 concept, and even though this is a totally different kind of car, you can certainly see those cues, especially in the wide fenders of the rear three-quarter section. The high-performance N version of the Elantra has already been spied, too, and it's going to look sick as hell.

The Elantra is slightly bigger than it used to be; 3.4 inches longer and 1.2 inches wider, to be exact, with 1.2 inches added to the wheelbase. Hyundai says the majority of that extra space goes to the second row, with gains in legroom (1.1 inches), headroom (0.7 inches) and shoulder room for rear-seat occupants, and now folks who accidentally had a kid will be able to better fit a rear-facing car seat.

Despite the extra size and funky angles, the 2027 Elantra still cuts through the air with ease, achieving a 0.26 coefficient of drag. Apparently, H-shaped daytime running lights and taillights are very aerodynamic. Who knew? The wedgey front end, also reminiscent of the N Vision 74, doesn't hurt either, and neither do the flush-mounted door handles.

It all helps explain why the Elantra is a real fuel economy winner whether you're looking at the entry-level gas motor or the optional hybrid. Fitted with 16-inch wheels, the 147-horsepower 2.0-liter inline-4, with the help of a CVT, will return up to 35 mpg combined, according to Hyundai. The 155-hp hybrid's 1.6-liter four-cylinder is mated to a six-speed dual-clutch transmission and 1.49-kWh battery, and Hyundai says it's going to achieve up to 53 mpg combined, which puts it firmly in "really, really good" territory. There's no word on other performance metrics right now, but I wouldn't expect anything too exciting, if I'm honest. The hybrid also comes with a Stay mode that lets you run accessories off the hybrid battery rather than the ICE motor when stationary for longer periods of time.

While the exterior is full of hard edges and sudden cuts, the interior is a far softer, more inviting place, one that wouldn't look out of position on a car that costs far more than the Elantra's currently unannounced price would suggest. Hyundai calls the furniture-inspired design ethos "Curve of Upholstery," and it's supposed to be all about comfort, simplicity, and minimizing driver distractions. It not only looks pretty thanks to interesting styling and materials choices, but it also feels nice to the touch with solid build quality.

Hyundai says Elantra is a "software-defined vehicle," which is pretty uncommon for an internal-combustion-powered car. Mostly Hyundai's spokespeople talk about its Pleos Connect operating system and its capabilities, like next-gen navigation (and AI assistance crap), and it explains why the interior's focal point is the 12.9-inch infotainment touchscreen in the center of the dash. The left section of the screen serves as a driver display showing speed and other pieces of vehicle information, while the rest of it is a regular infotainment screen with configurable widgets for media, maps, and everything else you can imagine — including things you can't imagine, since Pleos allows owners to download apps created by others.

Beneath the center screen are dual wireless 15-watt Qi 2.0 chargers and 100-watt ultra-fast USB-C charging ports for your many important devices, and you can run audio from said devices into an optional 12-speaker Bang & Olufsen audio system. Not too shabby.

Then, behind the steering wheel is a slim 9.9-inch display that is meant to keep the driver's field of vision uncluttered and only display critical information like speed, as well as radio, map directions or a few other things via widgets. We first saw both of these screens in the Tucson, and they make the Elantra feel far more tech-forward than a usual compact sedan would. Adding to that tech-forwardness is Hyundai's SmartSense suite of driver-assistance systems, which includes the classics like lane-keeping assist, lane centering, adaptive cruise control, forward collision avoidance and blind-spot monitoring.

At launch, the gas-only Elantra will come in SE, SEL Sport, and Limited flavors. As you may imagine, features and materials get nicer as you move up the range, but the 12.9-inch screen, adaptive cruise control, push-button start and a few other niceties are all standard from the get-go. Coming a bit later (no word on how much later) will be the 2028 Elantra Hybrid, which will come in SE Blue, SEL Sport, and Limited trims. It's the same deal as the gas car, but there's even more as standard, including dual-zone climate control and Stay mode.

I know that right now the Elantra is shiny and new, with its covers just pulled off at the 2026 LA Auto Show, and soon it'll face the sorts of abuse that all budget-friendly cars do. Before that happens, enjoy the Elantra and what it has to offer the world, because it's not very often an automaker swings for the fences on a cheap vehicle like this. Yes, vehicles like the Corolla, Civic and Mazda3 are very solid, but they're never exactly inspiring — certainly not from a design perspective, at least.

The eighth-generation Elantra elevates the segment, and it might force other automakers to rethink their budget vehicles as well. It certainly looks polarizing from the outside, and it won't be for everyone, but it's also distinctive, and that's something that is very hard to come by on a budget. If you're the type of person who appreciates that, plus a comfortable interior and tech that punches well above its weight class, then it's best you start getting ready now, because the Elantra is set to hit U.S. dealers in early 2027.

#5678. Europe Spent €16.5 Million Proving Again That Hydrogen Burns in a Turbine

Hydrogen burns. Turbines spin. Their exhaust can make steam. Kawasaki demonstrated hydrogen-fired electricity and heat production at Kobe Port Island in 2018, before Europe funded the first HYFLEXPOWER programme. Six years later, Siemens Energy is still issuing announcements about hydrogen combustion at a single turbine in a French paper mill. European and British taxpayers have supplied roughly €16.5 million for the two research programmes, and the same installation has generated at least 78 identified press appearances. Neither the grants nor the publicity have produced a commercial reason to make hydrogen from electricity and burn it for industrial electricity and steam.

The latest Siemens Energy announcement, dated November 16, 2026, describes an SGT-400 turbine at Smurfit Westrock’s Saillat-sur-Vienne paper mill operating on pure hydrogen through startup, load changes and full-load cogeneration. The equipment can operate under those conditions. Hydrogen combustion and heat recovery were already established. Extending the operating range of one manufacturer’s turbine has not changed hydrogen’s production cost, the losses involved in making it or the available alternatives. No second commercial installation has emerged from the programme.

Siemens’ own March 2024 technical article supplied the most important numbers. The electrolyzer installed at the paper mill produces 16.4 kg of hydrogen per hour. The turbine consumes about 810 kg per hour when producing 10 MW of electricity. Onsite production covers 2.02% of hourly fuel demand. Nearly 50 times that electrolyzer capacity would be needed to supply the turbine continuously at the stated operating point. Later testing used hydrogen brought to the site.

The 2023 campaign accumulated about 90 hours of hydrogen and natural-gas blending tests, including just over four hours on pure hydrogen. Siemens identified limited hydrogen availability as the constraint. The 2026 announcement supplies no cumulative full-load hydrogen operating hours, delivered fuel price or routine cost of electricity and steam. These are the figures an industrial customer needs before buying equipment. Announcing another combustion test avoids the question of who will supply hundreds of kilograms of affordable hydrogen every hour for years.

My complete TFIE Strategy Briefing investigation examines the funding records, Siemens’ published operating figures, the energy balance and an audited chronology of 78 press appearances surrounding the same turbine.

At an illustrative 50 kWh of electricity per kilogram of hydrogen, manufacturing the turbine’s 810 kg of hourly fuel requires approximately 40.5 MW of electricity. The turbine returns about 10 MW of electricity plus usable exhaust heat. Compression, storage and delivery add equipment and expense. The mill needs electricity and process steam; converting electricity into gas and burning it to recover those services introduces losses and costs that direct electrification avoids.

France is an especially poor location for this detour. RTE’s 2025 electricity review reports that 95.2% of French generation was low-carbon, with average generation emissions of 19.6 gCO₂e/kWh. Direct grid power can supply the electrical load. Industrial heat pumps, mechanical vapour recompression, electric boilers and thermal storage can supply process heat and steam in combinations designed around the mill’s operating requirements. The programme should have compared these complete systems before committing public money to more hydrogen turbine retrofits.

A paper mill in Finland is already doing the industrial work. Delfort’s Tervakoski plant has operated a Turboden heat pump and mechanical vapour-recompression installation since January 2026. It supplies about 12 MW of process steam at temperatures up to 170°C, with a reported coefficient of performance around two. It delivers useful steam without a hydrogen-production plant, hydrogen deliveries or a hydrogen-fired turbine. The exact plant integration will vary, but the alternative is operating commercially while HyCoFlex continues issuing test announcements.

The funding was directed at the wrong problem. HYFLEXPOWER received €10.48 million in EU support. HyCoFlex received another €4.44 million. A Siemens presentation identifies approximately €1.56 million more in UK support, bringing the public contribution across the programmes to about €16.48 million. Both programmes were designed around making existing gas-turbine cogeneration equipment compatible with hydrogen. The grants paid for additional turbine operating conditions instead of establishing that hydrogen was a sensible way to provide the plant’s energy.

The programme’s economics were weak before the second award. In October 2023, Siemens presented a scenario requiring electricity below €35/MWh to bring hydrogen fuel costs into parity with natural gas under its 2022 cost assumptions. The HYFLEXPOWER final workshop later examined favourable operating cases with hydrogen substitution and electrolyzer utilization both above 90%. European reporting also identified renewable electricity below €40/MWh as a condition for favourable deployment economics. France’s 2025 wholesale electricity averaged €61.1/MWh. Its negative-price hours were occasional. They could not supply a plant operating more than 90% of the time. These conditions were set out before the research programme ended, yet funding continued for more combustion trials.

Siemens also has a clear commercial interest in preserving turbine markets. Its 2025 presentation explicitly described protecting existing assets and future gas-turbine investments in a decarbonizing world as a benefit of hydrogen compatibility. A turbine supplier is entitled to pursue its products with its own money. The purpose of public industrial-decarbonization funding is to reduce emissions and costs, not to protect combustion-equipment sales from direct-electric competition.

The TFIE media audit counted 19 press appearances in 2020, 13 in the 2022 installation and blending phase, 35 around the 2023 tests and award, four in 2024 and seven through November 16, 2026. Those 78 appearances trace back to a handful of announcements about one installation. They are not 78 independent engineering advances or 78 deployments. The headline count swelled while the operating fleet did not.

Public funders should require equipment-neutral comparisons of delivered industrial energy services before underwriting another hydrogen retrofit. The evidence needed is familiar: a year’s reliable electricity and steam, actual operating cost, lifecycle emissions, fuel contracts, and performance against direct-electric alternatives. HyCoFlex has supplied more hydrogen-combustion publicity without establishing those outcomes. The problem was not that Europe failed to make a turbine burn hydrogen. It was that public money kept flowing after the relevant energy and economic questions already had answers.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing investigation contains the audited funding and media evidence, the 2% onsite hydrogen-supply calculation and the direct-electric industrial steam comparison. TFIE Strategy provides evidence-based assessments of industrial energy investments and public programmes.

The FDA approved dexmedetomidine sublingual film (Igalmi) for at-home use to treat agitation associated with schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, and bipolar I or II disorder in adults, maker Teva Pharmaceuticals announced.

#5675. Agents want the crown jewels: HPE and Daxa push governance down to the data layer

Enterprises are handing AI agents their most sensitive data, and governance is struggling to keep pace. Techniques such as semantic caching are emerging as a way to enforce controls inline without slowing agents down.

Moving agents from pilot to production means letting them read, change and even delete the records that matter most. That shift makes data access the central security question for agentic AI, according to Huseni Saboowala (pictured, right), co-founder and chief executive officer at Daxa Inc.

“For agents to really get to value, they need to be able to interact with your real enterprise data, and that includes your crown jewels, your intellectual property, your customer data in your [customer relationship management] and your proprietary trading algorithms,” he said. “That creates an unprecedented level of risk for enterprises because the agents are not just reading data; they’re also able to now go manipulate data at scale.”

Saboowala and Robin Braun (left), vice president of AI business development at Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., spoke with theCUBE’s Enterprise Editor, Paul Gillin, during coverage of SC26 on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. Daxa is a partner in HPE’s Unleash AI program, which offers pre-validated software on HPE Private Cloud AI. (* Disclosure below.)

Firewalls, data loss prevention and identity management still have a job to do. But they were built for users and applications, not software that reasons over data, Saboowala explained.

“Those agents are operating, though, at layer 8, what we call the cognitive layer,” he said. “This is where you have the prompts, the responses, the retrievals and the tool calls happening. Traditional tools really are not operating at this layer.”

Saboowala’s answer is reasoning-based access controls, backed by agents that flag abnormal behavior. HPE builds governance into its Private Cloud AI stack from the start, according to Braun.

“Being able to build in that governance from day one allows you to understand what is it going to look like so that … you’re not bolting it on later,” she said. “Instead, it’s a part of the workflow.”

Timing matters as much as policy. Offline governance arrives too late for agents working at machine speed, so enforcement must happen inline through semantic caching, specialized small language models and a distributed data plane, Saboowala explained. A regional bank that deployed Daxa with HPE has since connected its agents to source code and regulated customer data.

“I believe that the winners in this agent era are not just the ones who have the most [graphics processing units],” Saboowala said. “But they will be enterprises who have agents they can trust with their data.”

#5674. Should All Adults Be Screened for Lipoprotein(a)?

— Recent trial findings have provoked pushback of guidelines issued earlier this year

As a drug targeting lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), failed to prevent cardiovascular events in a closely-watched clinical trial, some experts are questioning recent national guidelines recommending that all adults be screened for it.

Back in March, a collaboration of 11 cardiology-related medical societies strongly recommended, for the first time, that all adults have their blood tested for Lp(a) -- also referred to as "Little a" -- at least once.

Higher scores, the committee said, reveal patients at much higher risk of developing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, incentivizing more aggressive management strategies, such as further lowering higher LDL cholesterol, HbA1c, body mass index, and other risks. The guidelines followed the European Atherosclerosis Society's similar recommendation in 2022 and the European Society of Cardiology's reinforcement in 2025.

But many prominent physicians say they are confused or are outright opposed to adding such a universal test. They argue that Lp(a), a heart disease risk marker known for years, is genetically inherited and not affected by LDL, diet, exercise or weight loss, and stays roughly the same through life.

They say the relationship to one's actual risk is unclear because Lp(a) may not necessarily be the cause of disease, but rather, may be related to something that is.

And there's not much one can do about a high score beyond what doctors normally recommend to reduce heart disease and stroke risks in their patients.

On top of that, CMS is allowing regional variation in whether Medicare covers the test, meaning that some seniors will have to pay for it out of pocket, depending on where they live.

"A lot of people are going to be very unnecessarily worried about a useless test that we should not be ordering or recommending in the first place," Rita Redberg, MD, MSc, a preventive cardiologist at the University of California San Francisco and former editor of JAMA Internal Medicine, told MedPage Today.

"It's certainly not going to make a difference in people once they pass age 50. You should be on a healthy lifestyle program no matter what your 'little a' is," Redberg said.

James Stein, MD, a cardiologist and emeritus professor at the University of Wisconsin in Madison, who has written several Substack blogs opposing universal use of the Lp(a) test, told MedPage Today the guidelines have "done a real disservice to the entire medical community by recommending widespread population screening because it creates a lot of anxiety."

"It also leads to a large downstream test cascade ... most of which is not indicated at all, and some of which actually puts you at additional risk for more problems," Stein said.

Then why did the committee make this recommendation?

"In general, there's been a 3-to-5-year push to do more Lp(a) testing, part of which is because there's a bias towards action. Let's do more. Let's prevent more disease," Stein said. "Part of it is because there's been some intellectual seeding, getting all of us ready for the Lp(a) lowering drugs, which a majority of people thought would show reduction in cardiac events."

In the HORIZON trial, the antisense oligonucleotide drug pelacarsen reduced Lp(a) levels, but it failed to reduce major cardiovascular events. That was a huge disappointment to researchers who had high hopes the drug would dramatically shrink cardiovascular death, strokes, and emergency cardiac interventions. If it had, it would have provided an important tool in the fight against cardiovascular disease.

But now, clinicians may find themselves at a loss for what to do about patients with a high Lp(a).

Stein remembers a recent clinic when three patients with no other cardiac risk factors "came in crying. Each one brought in a letter (showing their high scores)."

A woman in her early 70s had an extremely high score, above 350 nmol/l, with no family history and no other risk factors, and one of her children also had a high score, Stein said.

"'I can't believe I gave this to my child,' she told me," Stein said. "Now she is a healthy woman who feels like she has a sword dangling over her head. She does not."

Jason Goldman, MD, immediate past president of the American College of Physicians and an internist in Coral Springs, Florida, prefers recommending a coronary calcium CT score rather than an Lp(a), and was glad that at least the committee mentioned that option in its new guidelines.

"I am less enthusiastic about saying 'Little a' needs to be checked for everyone once because we don't have a treatment to lower it and improve outcomes, but we do have a treatment to lower LDL and cardiovascular disease," Goldman told MedPage Today. "CT calcium, I think, should be ordered on everyone, when appropriate."

He wishes the committee would reconsider its recommendation, especially in light of the HORIZON trial.

At the same time, several doctors told MedPage Today they welcomed the guidelines in their practices.

Jordan Rennicke, MD, a family medicine physician in Johnson City, Tennessee, orders Lp(a) draws for all his patients. And a few times, scores for patients without any risk factors including family history of cardiovascular disease have come back particularly high.

He knows that can "open up a can of worms," but he told MedPage Today he "values the information tremendously because then I can have a more informed discussion with my patients."

Karl Nadolsky, DO, an endocrinologist in Holland, Michigan, also checks all his patients. "It tells us who is carrying an extra inherited risk" that other scores don't show.

Roger Blumenthal, MD, chair of the guidelines committee and a Johns Hopkins cardiologist, said anticipation of positive pelacarsen trial results had nothing to do with the Lp(a) testing recommendation.

He said there's "overwhelming evidence from a multitude of studies that Lp(a) is a strong causal risk factor for atherosclerosis and aortic valve calcification and aortic valve stenosis."

The European societies' recommendations were particularly influential, he told MedPage Today. "We felt there are so many people who get cardiovascular disease at an earlier age than expected, and one common denominator is that they have a higher Lp(a). We felt it is a very reasonable test to do one time."

"Maybe some people say, well, you didn't have to have it as your strongest recommendation, you could make it a class 2A, and I certainly can understand that. But our colleagues across the pond have said the same thing ... that it's a good way to identify people who need to improve their lifestyle habits, that they may be at higher risk of atherosclerosis and aortic valve disease."

"And maybe we can do a better job of motivating people to improve their diet and exercise, and if you lower cholesterol significantly, you seem to neutralize most of the risk associated with a higher Lp(a)," he said.

Blumenthal emphasized that the "committee's guideline is not a rule. We're not saying that you have to do that. It's a simple blood test and it lets me know whether I take after my uncle or aunt who had a stroke or a heart attack at age 50. Then yeah, sure. Let's check it."

Blumenthal said in his own practice, he and many Johns Hopkins colleagues typically do not go by the new guideline to order Lp(a) blood screening for everybody. In his own practice, he orders it for patients who want to know their score, or if there's obvious risk factors like family history.

"There's a lot of well-meaning people on all sides," he said. "Some feel like if you measure anything, you're going to necessarily alarm people. But our feeling is that most people would like to know if they may have a factor that increases their risk, and if it does, then maybe that'll be the extra motivation."

"I understand there are other points of view and concerns," he said.

#5672. HLTH 2026: GLP-1 costs remain a challenge. A new CVS study aims to identify the right price

HLTH 2026: GLP-1 costs remain a challenge. A new CVS study aims to identify the right price" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Cost and access to GLP-1s remains a challenge, but the benefits of these drugs aren't in doubt.

A new study from CVS Health aims to quantify at what price a GLP-1 drug has generated enough savings elsewhere through improved clinical outcomes. The healthcare giant used anonymized claims data from Aetna members in fully insured plans and found savings from reduced hospital and medical spending, as well as improved health outcomes.

But those benefits weren't enough to offset the increased pharmaceutical spending at the current price point, the study found.

The study tracked a mix of members who took GLP-1s from 2023 to 2025, so some patients had three years of follow-up care and management.

Amy Compton-Phillips, M.D., chief medical officer at CVS, told Fierce Healthcare that part of the challenge in this equation is that these drugs gained steam as a treatment for obesity at a high price. And while those costs have come down, the reductions haven't yet been enough to offset the expenditures.

Another challenge for employers in particular—where GLP-1 coverage has been most in flux—is turnover, she said. While GLP-1s do drive significant improvements, an employer may not reap the benefit of the reduced cost if an employee moves to a different company before those are realized, even though they paid for the medication initially.

The study sought to identify a price point where those savings would be felt and landed at $350 per month over a three-year period. Achieving that, Compton-Phillips said, would likely lure employers into embracing broader GLP-1 coverage.

"For them, it might be really worthwhile to say, 'Hey, at this price point, I can afford to cover this for my employees, knowing that in the near term the savings will pay for my investment,'" she said.

The study found obesity rates declining after a 2022 peak, as well as a reduction of between 34% and 42% in hospitalizations over three years. Patients also had 14% lower odds of a serious cardiac event.

For patients who remained on the drugs for three years, their total medical spending decreased by $9,400, but associated pharmacy spending increased in tandem by $13,300, the study found.

Clinical improvements also fell off when patients were not able to remain adherent to the medication over several years, highlighting the importance of a wraparound approach that supports broader care management rather than simply prescribing a patient a GLP-1.

Compton-Phillips said CVS' own weight management program brings nutrition, peer coaching and other supports into the fold, in addition to the prescription. This is especially critical, she said, as evidence suggests weight gain is common after a patient stops taking their GLP-1, making behavior change key.

"At the moment, there's not great evidence that if you come off the drugs, you will maintain the weight loss," she said.

The CVS researchers said that the ultimate goal of the study was not to demand that all GLP-1 prescriptions repay their own costs, but to ensure that drug costs align with patient benefits and the broader cost of access. By lowering the net price of these products, more people can access them, the study concludes.

"These drugs make people's lives better, and I want to give them out," Compton-Phillips said. Doing so becomes a challenge, though, "at the price they are today," she said.

#5671. Quadruple Agonist Reduced Weight Without Major Muscle Loss in Mid-Stage Trial

— Once-daily oral agent also showed favorable tolerability

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. -- An investigational oral quadruple receptor agonist led to substantial weight loss with preservation of lean mass, a randomized phase II trial presented here showed.

By week 13, the two highest tested doses of NA-931 -- 150 mg and 120 mg -- led to reductions in mean body weight of 13.8% and 11.3%, respectively, compared with a reduction of 1.9% with placebo among adults with obesity or overweight and weight-related comorbidities (P=0.001 and P=0.002).

Participants receiving the two lowest doses -- 60 mg and 90 mg -- lost 5.5% and 8.7% of baseline body weight, respectively, according to Lloyd L. Tran, PhD, of developer Biomed Industries in San Jose, California, and colleagues.

The topline findings "support the potential of NA-931 as a first-in-class oral quadruple receptor agonist for weight loss, with promising efficacy and tolerability," Tran said at the ObesityWeek annual meeting, adding that the results also "suggest potential muscle preservation."

Using dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) measurements, which estimate lean soft tissue, including skeletal muscle, organs, and water (though changes do not directly establish shifts in muscle function), lean mass decreased by 1.7% over 13 weeks among participants treated with NA-931.

For context, longer-duration trials of the GLP-1 agonist semaglutide (Wegovy) over 68 weeks and the dual GLP-1/GIP agonist tirzepatide (Zepbound) over 72 weeks reported reductions in lean mass of 13.2% and 10.9%, respectively. According to a 2025 meta-analysis of 22 randomized trials of semaglutide and tirzepatide, including 2,258 patients, lean mass reductions made up roughly 25% of total weight lost.

"We believe we are entering an era of post-GLP-1 where there is a need for sustainable obesity management" that pairs meaningful weight loss with preserved muscle strength, Tran said. That preservation is particularly critical for older adults, he noted, as muscle mass naturally declines by roughly 3% to 8% per decade after age 30 and accelerates after age 60.

NA-931 is a small molecule that targets four receptors: insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon. Because the compound readily crosses the blood-brain barrier, only a low dose is needed for efficacy, Tran explained, which may contribute to its favorable tolerability profile.

In the 150-mg NA-931 group, rates of gastrointestinal adverse events -- a common side effect of GLP-1-based therapies -- were only slightly higher than with placebo, including nausea (12.5% vs 10.3%; all cases mild), vomiting (8.3% vs 6.9%), and diarrhea (8.3% vs 6.9%). No participants in the 150-mg arm discontinued treatment.

By comparison, pivotal trials of semaglutide and tirzepatide reported nausea in 44.2% (vs 17.4% on placebo) and 24.6% to 33.3% (vs 9.5% on placebo) of participants, respectively.

This multicenter, double-blind trial enrolled 125 adults with obesity or overweight and weight-related comorbidities. Participants were randomized to receive once-daily oral NA-931 at 60 mg, 90 mg, 120 mg, or 150 mg, or placebo. Mean participant age across the groups ranged from 41.9 to 46.7 years. Most were female (62.5% to 66.6%) and white (62.5% to 68.9%). Mean baseline weight was 212 to 220.9 lb and mean body mass index was 34.4 to 37.8.

Patients in the 150-mg group also saw a modest reduction in HbA1c levels (-0.2%).

Tran said Biomed Industries is advancing NA-931 into phase III clinical testing.

#5670. Volvo Trucks Realizes Universal Dream Of Life-Size Tonka Trucks With New Tech

Remote control trucks are cool and all, but haven't you ever wanted to remote control something bigger? Realer? Well, Volvo Trucks has your number. The company just introduced a new feature that allows operators to remote-control their own heavy-duty vocational truck — so long as it is on a job site, that is, and going under five miles per hour.

Volvo's new tech, Remote Steer, is just that — a way to steer and control the company's new VNX heavy-duty truck from a gaming style control from outside the vehicle. It may sound like a party trick, but Volvo actually makes a good case for its use: Rather than relying on communication between a driver and a spotter for precision jobs, like aligning a trailer hitch or pouring concrete, Remote Steer allows one person to do both jobs. A worker can stand behind their truck, at the trailer hitch, and use the remote to back the truck up perfectly without any risk of anyone saying "No, no, my left."

It wouldn't be Volvo Trucks if safety wasn't first and foremost in mind. The operator is responsible for switching on the system in the cab and linking the cab to a VIN-specific remote control. The remote control is married to only one VIN number, so there can't be an switch-em-up which could result in everything from hilarious shenanigans to untimely death. There is also a very limited range on the controller, as well as emergency stop buttons on both truck and controller. You'll also need to have all the latest and greatest Volvo Trucks tech to make it work, like Volvo Dynamic Steering, I-Shift transmission, electronic braking system, and a Body Builder Module. If you have that stuff, you can get the module installed aftermarket at any time.

Will this truck replace workers on the job site? Probably not. Ideally, Remote Steer will be used on job sites as a way to help existing workers rather than as a way to replace them. If that's the use case the tech sees, it'll likely be a genuine boon to the folks who have to do precision maneuvers on their trucks all day long. Then again, you might not see it at all, as Volvo Trucks, while sold worldwide to the tune of 120,000 trucks last year, has a smaller footprint here in the U.S than competitors like Mack (which is now a part of Volvo Trucks) or Kenworth trucks.

Either way, we hope we get invited to this press drive. Five miles an hour sounds like peanuts and, on the road, it is, but you don't need much more to dig around in a life-size sandbox with your buddies. Volvo's next move should be expanding to front loaders, excavators and Volvo Trucks-branded microbreweries that allow you to dig around and drink an IPA at the same time. The money would print itself.

#5669. Humana launches national provider Gold Card program

Humana launches national provider Gold Card program" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Humana is continuing its push to reform prior authorization with the launch of a national provider gold card program.

The program will go into effect on Dec. 1, the company announced Tuesday. It will focus initially on MRI, CT and MRA imaging as well as physical and occupational therapy. Through the program, eligible providers will no longer need to secure a prior authorization approval and can instead use a streamlined process.

Humana estimates that about 50,000 providers will qualify for the program. Eligible providers must be able to demonstrate a proven track record of high-quality care and patient outcomes.

Traci Granston, M.D., vice president of clinical innovation and trend at Humana, told Fierce Healthcare in an exclusive interview that prior authorization and other utilization management approaches are key in ensuring that patients receive the appropriate care.

However, lengthy decision times and other barriers can create a painful friction. So for providers that consistently demonstrate that they are aligned with clinical guidelines, the gold cards can remove that guardrail.

"If they're following those guidelines and providing appropriate care, prior auths don't really serve a purpose for them," Granston said.

The insurer conducted a pilot earlier this year with about 400 provider organizations and approximately 8,000 clinicians. Through that process, the team conducted interviews with clinicians and office staff who shared their desire for fewer administrative burdens and a simpler experience.

Those insights shaped the broader launch, Humana said, and the insurer intends to continue to iterate and evolve the gold card program over time, including by adding new service lines. It's not uncommon for a program to roll out that aims to support providers, but their voice is less often at the table in shaping what the experience looks like to ensure that their pain points are being addressed.

Granston said that the team is examining more time-sensitive services that could fit within the program, for example.

"For our top-performing providers, we would like to essentially get out of the way and let them continue to care for our members," she said.

The gold card program builds on Humana's existing work to reform prior authorization, including a streamlined approval process for electronic submissions that took effect in January of this year. Under this initiative, Humana responds within one business day in 95% of electronic prior authorization cases.

The insurer also announced earlier this month that it would join forces with athenahealth to accelerate the use of electronic prior authorization. Through the partnership, more of the process is embedded directly in the provider's workflow, streamlining the experience for them at the point of care.

Granston said that the goal is to make it easier to surface the data necessary to make an approval and enable that to occur in real time. This also means that fewer people have to be dedicated to the work of submissions and approval.

"When the information exists, you don't really need all these people to be touching it," she said.

#5668. Tau Therapy Shows Continued Benefit at 2 Years in Alzheimer's

— Open-label extension data suggest diranersen's treatment effects may build over time

Diranersen, an investigational antisense oligonucleotide therapy that targets tau, continued to show benefits for 96 weeks, data from the open-label extension of the phase II CELIA trial suggested.

At 2 years, diranersen continued to slow clinical decline across measures of cognition, function, and disease progression, reported Lawren VandeVrede, MD, PhD, of the University of California San Francisco, at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease (CTAD) conference in Boston.

A 60-mg dose twice a year showed the largest effects; with that regimen, participants had a 1.09-point treatment difference in Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) score at 96 weeks, surpassing the 76-week CDR-SB score, VandeVrede observed. CDR-SB scores can range from 0 to 18, and a 1-point change is considered meaningful, he added.

Treatment effects were calculated by comparing 60 participants who received diranersen during CELIA's placebo-controlled phase and stayed on the same dose through 2 years with 115 people who were originally assigned to placebo and then moved into the study's open-label extension.

On the CDR-SB, the treatment effect grew from 26% at week 76 to 38% at week 96, VandeVrede said.

Other measurements of cognition and function also improved from 76 to 96 weeks, he added. "The increasing separation observed between 18 months and 2 years is remarkable," VandeVrede noted.

Safety findings through week 96 were generally consistent with data from the placebo-controlled period. The most frequent adverse events were procedural pain, post-lumbar puncture syndrome, headache, and confusional state. Most confusional state events were mild or moderate, occurred within 7 days of dosing, and resolved within 7 days of onset.

Diranersen targets microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT) RNA. It is designed to reduce both intracellular and extracellular tau.

CELIA was a phase II dose-ranging study of diranersen in individuals with early Alzheimer's disease. It enrolled 416 participants with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease or mild Alzheimer's disease dementia who had not previously received anti-amyloid therapy.

The study evaluated three doses of diranersen administered intrathecally over the 18-month placebo-controlled treatment period: 60 mg every 6 months, 115 mg every 6 months, and 115 mg every 3 months.

The primary endpoint was an assessment of dose response for change from baseline on CDR-SB scores at week 76. All diranersen doses tested in CELIA slowed cognitive decline, but because the lowest dosage performed best, the drug missed its primary endpoint of demonstrating a clear dose response. The ongoing open-label extension study is evaluating the long-term safety, tolerability, and durability of diranersen's clinical benefit.

"CELIA gave the field its first evidence from a randomized trial that lowering tau may slow cognitive decline, and today's 2-year data suggest that benefit may build over time," said Laura Nisenbaum, PhD, interim chief science officer of the Alzheimer's Drug Discovery Foundation in New York City, who wasn't involved with the study.

"The lowest dose appeared to perform best, but its safety and clinical benefit will need to be confirmed in a larger phase III trial," she noted. "Importantly, diranersen also lowered tau without affecting amyloid, making it a promising candidate to pair with anti-amyloid therapies as the field works toward combination treatments that address the full pathobiology of Alzheimer's."

New data from the placebo-controlled treatment period presented at CTAD showed that, at 18 months, the twice-yearly 60-mg diranersen group had favorable memory, orientation, and executive function scores compared with participants on other doses. Biomarker analyses showed that diranersen reduced tau PET signals and lowered soluble tau biomarker levels.

#5667. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.
